title: First week with Priya
description: Demo conversation (synthetic, for the demo account). Alex tells Priya the studio met the counter halfway, describes building a physical prototype in the first week, how the imposter feelings are easing and a Stoic morning reminder that helped, then returns to the prototype.

utterances.text: Okay, first week at the studio. Tell me everything.
It was so good. Tiring, but good. Oh, and I never told you how the money ended. They met my counter halfway.
Halfway! Alex, that's great. So you're close to your old salary?
Close enough. And the work is so much better that I stopped caring about the last bit.
So what did they have you doing? Onboarding videos?
No, straight in. I'm building a physical prototype for the science center gallery. A tide pool table where kids push water around and little projected crabs run away.
Wait, you're building it? Like, with your hands?
Foam board, a cheap projector and a lot of hot glue.
That's the opposite of claim forms.
Totally. On Thursday we put it in the lobby and watched two kids use it. One of them just slapped it for ten minutes.
Is that good or bad?
Good, apparently! My lead said slapping means it's fun. Reading the label is the part nobody does.
Ha. And the imposter thing? You were so sure they'd realize they hired the wrong person.
Honestly, it's easing. By Wednesday I noticed nobody there has built this exact thing either. And the screen stuff transfers. A gallery is just a big, slow interface.
That's what Dana told you, right?
Word for word. But what helped most was your fault.
Mine? What did I do?
The Stoic stuff. I started a morning reminder. On the bus I read one line of Marcus Aurelius, then tell myself, today some things will go wrong, and that's fine.
Like his line about meeting rude, ungrateful people?
My version. Today the glue won't hold, someone will change the brief, and I'll still do good work.
That's adorable. Does it actually work?
On the bad days, yes. On Tuesday the client changed the table height and I didn't spiral. I just thought, not up to me, what's next.
Look at you. Marcus would be proud.
Ha. He'd tell me to be less petty about the table height.
Okay, back to the crabs. What happens to the prototype now?
Next week we test it with a school group. Twenty kids, which is either great data or total chaos.
Both, probably. And after that?
If it works, they build the real one in steel and glass, and my foam board goes in the recycling.
Take a picture of it first. Your first thing people can walk around.
Already did. It's my lock screen.
